claims.statement: RLS authorization is decided by the app_private.security-definer helper chain (current_clerk_user_id → current_profile_id → current_role / can_access_tenant → can_manage_tenant / can_read_batch / can_trainer_write_batch) rather than by any role string the application compares, and identity is read only from auth.jwt() ->> 'sub' so no custom JWT claim can widen access.
Deactivating a profile drops access on the next request because current_profile_id() and can_access_tenant() both require profiles.is_active = true, so no separate revocation list exists.

public.platform_admins has RLS enabled with deliberately no policy, so the app can only learn the caller's platform-admin status through the boolean-only definer RPC public.current_user_is_platform_admin(), which is why the role cannot be self-granted through any application path.

createSupabaseServerClient() authenticates with the anon key plus Clerk's native third-party-auth accessToken callback that re-invokes getToken() with no template argument, so an expired token is refreshed instead of reused from a static Authorization header.

The accessToken callback throws the exported NO_CLERK_TOKEN_MESSAGE sentinel when Clerk issues no token, so the caller's catch maps a missing session to sync-failed instead of letting RLS answer every query with a silently empty anon read; the sentinel also distinguishes 'not signed in' from 'token rejected'.

The service-role client is confined to lib/supabase/service.ts and reserved for the webhook, which has no Clerk session to scope it by; every other path uses the anon-key client so RLS stays the boundary.

A JS tenant check is banned as access control even when correct because the failure mode is drift rather than a leak; the one sanctioned shape is a tenant_id = scope.tenantId filter from a TenantScope, which only selects among schools RLS already allows.

scopeForCode builds a scope only from profile.tenants, itself an RLS-scoped read, so a foreign or unknown URL code yields null rather than a scope; resolveRouteScope exposes that as a four-way cached result whose non-ok arms the segment layout renders, and requireScope returns null instead of throwing notFound() because layout and page render in parallel.

The tenant-access verdict is joined into route code from app/ because it composes two private data/ layers: billing fetches the profile for the trainer redirect and derives deriveTenantAccess from that same snapshot rather than through a tenancy helper.

The admin check in the create-user Server Action is defence in depth rather than the boundary — RLS rejects a non-admin's INSERT — but it is load-bearing on the Clerk invitation branch, which has no RLS behind it.

TenantAccess has three values where none means no membership and unknown means the check could not run; unknown must never be rendered as none because 'we could not check' is not 'you have no school'.
deriveTenantAccess maps a missing profile row to none and a failed or unconfigured profile read to unknown, so an unverified read is never normalised into a fact.

withTenantAccess replaces only an ok snapshot: sync-failed and unconfigured pass through untouched so a real failure is never masked by the tidier 'no school' story, and unknown changes nothing because an unverified verdict must not rewrite a successful read.

The dashboard's guardState checks a zero-row sync failure ahead of the no-tenant-access and empty arms, because a failed fetch yields zero rows and would otherwise satisfy a misleading empty state and swallow the sync-failed banner (rule 19); billing instead returns null from the page on a non-ok scope, which is also its no-tenant-access shape and is safe only because a zero-membership caller has no school URL to reach the segment with.

Viewer read-only is server denial, not hidden controls: viewer appears in no write policy because can_manage_tenant() requires admin or coordinator and can_trainer_write_batch() requires trainer, so a viewer can replay a request and still be refused.
Role authority is profiles.role through resolveTrustedRole, never Clerk metadata and never the ?role= presentation override; toOfficeRole collapses anything unrecognised to least-privileged viewer.

Redirects that enforce the trainer omission are gated on resolveTrustedRole, so a real trainer cannot request ?role=admin and skip them; billing resolves billingRole from resolveRouteRole only after the trusted-role redirect.
Trainer trimming has two non-interchangeable halves: RLS narrows rows through can_read_batch so a trainer's fetches return only assigned batches, and the financial DTO fields are omitted server-side.

The trainer server-omission half is a domain strip plus prop absence, not CSS: /trainer fetches with no scope and runs deriveTrainerMetrics, which strips the billing keys from the object, then renders MetricsRow (a thin wrapper taking TrainerDashboardMetrics) and a KpiSummary with no billing prop, so NextBillingCard is never emitted; the school dashboard passes billing={metrics} instead.

learner_details exists as a one-to-one table because RLS filters rows and not columns: the T2MIS contact, birth-date, employer and salary fields would otherwise be one API call from any assigned trainer, so they live in a table whose read policy names admin, coordinator and viewer and deliberately omits trainers.

New migrations are additive and each new table or function needs its own grant, because the base migration's grant over all public tables and all app_private functions was a one-time statement over the objects that then existed.
RLS isolation tests run against real Supabase with no mocks, but rule 36 makes them permission-gated against the single hosted project, so the checked-in policy text remains intent until verified.

Every authorization proposition on this page rests on reading migrations and route code: rule 35's real-Supabase RLS tests cannot simply be run because there is one hosted project and no staging, rule 36 makes any statement against it permission-gated, and no tests/integration/ or tests/security/ directory exists, so the unit suite pins only the JS verdicts.

The server action re-resolves the school from the URL code and never reads a tenant id from the form, takes the role from profiles.role via resolveTrustedRole, and states that both checks are defence in depth — the batches UPDATE policy is the boundary and matches zero rows for anyone else, surfaced as the shared conflict-or-denied status.

An unscoped client is safe only because a policy narrows it: getBatchesSnapshot appends the tenant filter only when an id is passed, and /trainer and /overview both pass none — correct for can_read_batch's trainer narrowing and can_access_tenant's membership narrowing respectively; /overview must not be path-scoped because it groups every school by school rather than summing under one name (audit I1).

withTenantAccess lives in domain/ rather than in route code because another module's data/ is private (rule 8); the two screens that already hold a profile snapshot (billing, report) call deriveTenantAccess on it directly instead of fetching membership twice, and the rest use tenantAccessOf off the scope they were handed.

lib/supabase/server.ts is an anon-key Supabase client whose accessToken callback re-invokes Clerk's getToken() with no template argument, so RLS resolves identity from the session's `sub` claim against the database rather than from any app-supplied claim; a null token throws the exported NO_CLERK_TOKEN_MESSAGE sentinel that /api/debug/auth-check matches and data layers surface as sync-failed.

tests/unit/supabase-server.test.ts pins both the throw-on-missing-token behavior and the absence of a static Authorization header, so drifting the sentinel message silently breaks the /api/debug/auth-check diagnostic.
app_private.current_profile_id() selects only on profiles.is_active = true, so deactivation (what the Clerk user.deleted webhook writes) drops access at the next request with no revocation list.

modules/tenancy/domain/scope.ts builds a TenantScope only from profile.tenants, comparing codes case-insensitively and returning null for a foreign or unknown code, so an unrecognized URL code never falls back to an all-schools scope; tests/unit/tenant-scope.test.ts pins that one-way door.

`tenant_id` appears nowhere in app/ route code: every page passes scope.tenantId into a module data/ function, and the filter itself is written only in the query (getBatchesSnapshot and setBatchRqmCode, both annotated that it is not authorization), so copying the .eq into a route or filtering returned rows in JS is the drift RULES rule 2 describes.

The /t/<code> segment layout resolves the route scope and renders distinct EmptyState/NoTenantAccessState branches for unknown, no-tenant-access and not-a-member instead of throwing a 404, while pages below call requireScope (the same cached read) for the validated scope.

deriveTenantAccess maps not-found to `none` (a signed-in user with no profile row has no membership either way) and sync-failed/unconfigured to `unknown`, because 'we could not check' must never render as 'you have no school'; tests/unit/tenant-access.test.ts pins both.

withTenantAccess(snapshot, access) rewrites only an `ok` snapshot to no-tenant-access, leaving sync-failed and unconfigured untouched so the tidier 'you belong to no school' story cannot bury a rule-19 sync-failed banner, and leaving `unknown` a no-op so an unverified verdict never rewrites a successful read; the test pins both.

Screens guard failures before emptiness in both mechanisms: the dashboard's guardState checks `syncFailed && batchCount === 0` ahead of the no-tenant-access and empty arms, and billing/report use the same precedence as a `syncFailed && batches.length === 0` early return placed before the no-tenant-access branch.

Billing and report are the newer, preferred shape for the tenant-access verdict: each already holds a profile snapshot for the trainer redirect and derives the verdict from that snapshot (`profileSnapshot ? deriveTenantAccess(profileSnapshot) : 'unknown'`, so a null snapshot yields unknown, not none) rather than re-reading membership, then passes it to the same fold.

The `if (!resolved) return null` immediately after requireScope on a page is safe only because the segment layout already rendered the non-ok scope states and layouts and pages render in parallel, so the null never reaches a guard ladder.

The verdict is obtained through three doors — tenantAccessOf(profile) off a validated scope for the six scoped sections, deriveTenantAccess on a snapshot the route already holds for billing and report, and resolveTenantAccess() for /overview and legacy redirects — all converging on domain/ so the not-found→none and unknown≠none rules hold regardless of entry point.

Every scoped office page routes through requireScope, which performs the `profile.role === 'trainer'` redirect for the whole segment, so a new page that skips it (calling resolveRouteScope or getProfileSnapshot directly) hands a trainer the full office batch payload that RLS narrows by row but does not strip by column.

Viewer is read-only at the database, not merely hidden: can_manage_tenant() requires admin or coordinator, can_trainer_write_batch() requires trainer plus assignment to the row's batch, and the admin-write policies test `current_role() = 'admin'` directly, so no write predicate admits a viewer.

The role driving that denial is read from profiles.role only: resolveTrustedRole(null) returns null instead of falling back to the Clerk user object that the tenant-scope test mocks as an admin, so the test would fail if the resolver started consulting Clerk.

The t/[tenantCode] server action re-resolves the school from the URL code on the server (never reading a tenant id from the form) and takes the role from profiles.role via resolveTrustedRole, but documents both as defence in depth: the boundary is the batches UPDATE policy, whose zero-row match for a non-admin surfaces as the deliberately ambiguous conflict-or-denied status shared with a concurrent edit.

An unscoped client is safe only because a policy narrows it: getBatchesSnapshot appends the tenant filter only when an id is passed, and /trainer and /overview pass none because RLS already narrows rows to a trainer's assignments (can_read_batch) or an admin's memberships (can_access_tenant).

/overview is the one office screen that must not be scoped by path: it reads every school the caller belongs to and labels results by grouping on profile.tenants in application code while the row set stays RLS's, which is the audit I1 shape.

The trainer boundary is enforced by redirects keyed on resolveTrustedRole, never the ?role= preview: /billing and /report redirect('/trainer') before fetching, and /overview redirects non-admins to /dashboard.

/trainer fetches with no scope and passes rows through deriveTrainerMetrics, which deletes the billing keys from the object so they are absent at runtime rather than merely typed away; the test asserts the four keys are missing and that no billing date survives JSON.stringify.

The trainer KPI row omits billing by a missing prop, not a flag or CSS: MetricsRow takes TrainerDashboardMetrics and never passes `billing`, while KpiSummary is shared and renders NextBillingCard only when `billing` is supplied by the school dashboard.

/trainer sits outside the tenant segment because a trainer's slice is not one school, and its KPI row is gated on the metrics value, so a failed snapshot renders no row at all rather than a zeroed one.

Rule 5's RLS half is can_read_batch(), which narrows a trainer to their own assigned batches, while learner_details reads only for admin/coordinator/viewer because RLS filters rows and not columns; the omission half is implemented as object-level stripping, not a hideBilling helper.

Rules 1 and 2 are [review]-enforced with no automated check, so neither fails lint, typecheck or the test suite, and the evidence base is migrations plus route code because there is one hosted project, no staging, and no tests/integration or tests/security directory.
